query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: For representative high-entropy alloys (including FCC, BCC, and refractory HEAs), an integrated high-throughput experimental setup that combines DSC/DTA with in-situ synchrotron XRD and high-temperature imaging can accurately determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting with uncertainties less than ±10 K, ±5 kJ/mol, and ±2% respectively, when measured under inert atmosphere conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A set of as-cast, polycrystalline high-entropy alloys (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi, Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0, etc.) with controlled grain sizes and minimal oxidation.
generation.intervention: Subject each alloy sample to a controlled heating protocol (e.g., 10 K/min with intermittent relaxation periods) under an inert gas (Argon or Nitrogen), while simultaneously recording calorimetric heat flow (via DSC/DTA), diffraction patterns (via synchrotron XRD), and real-time volume/morphology changes (via high-temperature imaging).
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted in a high-temperature furnace within an inert atmosphere; temperature range spanning from room temperature up to beyond the solidus, capturing the entire melting process; calibration against standard reference materials.
generation.structural_mediator: The phase change from solid to liquid is indicated by a distinct endothermic peak (latent heat) in DSC/DTA, an abrupt change in diffraction patterns (loss of long-range order) in XRD, and a measurable volume change from imaging analysis.
generation.mechanism: As the sample is heated, its atomic lattice remains stable until reaching the melting point, where latent heat absorption (fusion enthalpy) triggers a rapid collective atomic rearrangement, resulting in measurable entropy increase and discontinuous volume expansion or contraction. The integration of the three techniques allows for deconvolution of the latent (fusion) characteristics from the sensible heat contributions, ensuring accurate thermodynamic determination.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated method will yield melting temperatures within ±10 K of established values, latent fusion enthalpy measurements within ±5 kJ/mol, and volume change measurements with an error margin below ±2% compared to baseline references (e.g., results from conventional DSC/DTA and validated MD simulations). Consistency across different HEA compositions will confirm its applicability.
generation.baseline: Established literature values from conventional DSC/DTA experiments and validated atomistic simulations (e.g., data from PMC7513177 and PMC8956691) for benchmark HEAs.
generation.boundary: This integrated approach is applicable for HEAs that form predominantly single-phase or well-characterized multiphase structures. It may be limited by cases with extreme segregation or oxidation issues and alloys with nonstandard phase behaviors not captured by diffraction.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties arise from instrumental calibration (±5-10 K in temperature, ±5% in heat flow), sample preparation variability, and potential local compositional heterogeneities. These are minimized through rigorous calibration and repeated measurements.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct an inter-laboratory round-robin experiment on a standard HEA (e.g., equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi) using the integrated DSC/DTA, synchrotron XRD, and high-temperature imaging setup. Compare the measured melting temperature, latent heat, entropy change, and volume change to benchmark values obtained from conventional DSC/DTA and established MD simulations.
measurements: DSC/DTA heat flow curves to identify endothermic peaks corresponding to melting
In-situ synchrotron XRD patterns to detect loss of crystallinity at melting
High-temperature imaging data to quantify volumetric changes during melting
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated method produces melting temperature deviations greater than ±10 K, latent fusion enthalpy discrepancies exceeding ±5 kJ/mol, or volume change measurements outside a ±2% error margin compared to benchmark values, then the proposed approach is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe determined the entropy of high entropy alloys by investigating single-crystalline nickel and five high entropy alloys: two fcc-alloys, two bcc-alloys and one hcp-alloy. Since the configurational entropy of these single-phase alloys differs from alloys using a base element, it is important to quantify the entropy. Using differential scanning calorimetry, cp-measurements are carried out from −170 °C to the materials’ solidus temperatures TS. From these experiments, we determined the thermal entropy and compared it to the configurational entropy for each of the studied alloys. We applied the rule of mixture to predict molar heat capacities of the alloys at room temperature, which were in good agreement with the Dulong-Petit law. The molar heat capacity of the studied alloys was about three times the universal gas constant, hence the thermal entropy was the major contribution to total entropy. The configurational entropy, due to the chemical composition and number of components, contributes less on the absolute scale. The field of high-entropy alloys continues to grow every year, and with this growth comes an enormous amount of never before seen alloy systems with unknown liquid state behavior. As previously shown, neutron imaging can be a very useful technique to elucidate the liquid state behavior of molten alloy systems. With the application of this technique to high-entropy alloys, in-situ imaging of liquid state miscibility has been observed for the first time with the equiatomic additions of Ni to the immiscible CoCrCu system. The current results show the following: Neutron imaging can be utilized to image liquid state behavior in high-entropy alloys. Imaging was carried out on equiatomic CoCrCu buttons with equiatomic additions of Ni such that when melting occurred between the alloying elements, full miscibility was achieved. In-situ neutron imaging was successfully utilized to image in-situ alloying of Ni into an immiscible CoCrCu system. The synthesis of the CoCrCuNi alloy inside the high-temperature furnace was fully imaged via a movie-like sequence of carefully timed radiographs to display the melting/alloying process. papers.title: How atoms of polycrystalline Nb20.6Mo21.7Ta15.6W21.1V21.0 refractory high-entropy alloys rearra
papers.approach: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using the second-nearest neighbor modified embedded-atom method (2NN MEAM) to study both single crystal and polycrystalline configurations during heating.
papers.findings: Observed an abrupt drop in density and an enthalpy maximum in the single crystal between ~2910–2940 K. In polycrystalline systems, a two-stage melting process was evident: initial pre-melting at the grain boundaries followed by complete melting of the grain interiors. Grain size impacts the melting temperature with smaller grains exhibiting more pronounced melting precursor behavior.
papers.mechanism: Grain boundary atoms first acquire enough kinetic energy to leave equilibrium positions (pre-melting), which triggers a cascade of local structural rearrangements—a collective atomic reorganization process leading to full melting.

papers.title: Entropy Determination of Single-Phase High Entropy Alloys with Different Crystal Structures over a Wide Temperature Range.
papers.system: Various high-entropy alloys with FCC, BCC, and HCP structures
papers.approach: Experimental measurement of temperature-dependent molar heat capacity (cp) using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) over a wide temperature range. The method uses extrapolation (Debye T³ law) at low temperatures and comparison with the Dulong–Petit law near room temperature.
papers.findings: Determined that thermal entropy (from vibrational contributions) largely dominates over configurational entropy in absolute scale; the vertical offset between thermal and total entropy indicates the impact of atomic configuration. Melting-related enthalpy changes (fusion enthalpy) are measurable using the abrupt rise in cp near the solidus.
papers.mechanism: Separation of entropy contributions: vibrational (thermal) entropy defined by atomic heat capacities and configurational entropy governed by element mixing; these together explain solid-state stabilization and the changes at incipient melting.

papers.title: Computational property predictions of Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics (MC/MD) simulations to model annealing treatments. The method tracks the evolution of potential energy and uses neighbor bond counting statistics to estimate configurational entropy contributions and changes in the Gibbs free energy (ΔG).
papers.findings: The thermodynamic evolution shows a continuous and smooth reduction in ΔG during MC/MD swaps. It was found that configurational entropy can contribute up to 40% of the ΔH reduction, and that equilibrium is approached after sufficient swaps (e.g., beyond 20 swaps, ΔG converges within 2.5%).
papers.mechanism: Local chemical clustering (short-range order, SRCs) alters bond statistics and energetics, promoting changes in both enthalpy and entropy. The balance between enthalpy reduction and entropy increase dictates the progression toward a lower free-energy state.

papers.title: Predictive multiphase evolution in Al-containing high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: Al-containing high-entropy alloys (multi-phase systems with BCC/B2 features)
papers.approach: High-throughput first-principles calculations to parameterize a simple model integrated into Monte Carlo simulations. This approach focuses on phase evolution including order-disorder transitions and melting-related phase separations, complemented by experimental techniques (DSC, in situ microscopy).
papers.findings: Reproduced the major features of Al-containing phase evolution; specifically, B2 ordering and phase separation phenomena at predicted temperatures (~565 ± 30 °C for ordering and a B2/BCC separation near 600 °C) observed by DSC and microscopy validate the computational predictions.
papers.mechanism: Competition between enthalpic preferences for ordered intermetallic phases and entropic stabilization of disordered solid solutions drives the phase evolution and influences melting behavior.

papers.title: Thermal Analysis of High-Entropy Rare Earth Oxides.
papers.system: High-entropy rare earth sesquioxides ((La,Sm,Dy,Er,RE)2O3 systems, where RE = Nd, Gd, or Y)
papers.approach: A combination of splat quenching, high-temperature differential thermal analysis (DTA), synchrotron X-ray diffraction, and CALPHAD modeling to determine phase transitions, melting points, enthalpy of fusion, and volume changes upon melting.
papers.findings: Identified three reversible high-temperature phase transitions and measured melting points (e.g., 2456 ± 12 °C for (La,Sm,Dy,Er,Nd)2O3). The experiments also quantified volume changes associated with transitions that were consistent with solid–liquid mixing behavior and nonideal effects.
papers.mechanism: Nonideal mixing between the rare earth oxides in both the solid and liquid states, as well as potential local ordering, leads to deviations from ideal behavior that affect melting temperature and fusion properties.

papers.title: Thermal and Structural Analysis of a High-Entropy Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 Alloy-Infl
papers.approach: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) under varied cooling conditions (slow cooling, accelerated cooling, and rapid quenching) coupled with X-ray diffraction (XRD), SEM, TEM, and Mössbauer spectroscopy to capture fusion events and phase transformations.
papers.findings: DSC curves revealed distinct endothermic peaks corresponding to phase transitions and melting. Notably, the melting process showed a large energy absorption (−70.53 J/g) and endothermic peak starting around 1297.7 K, while distinct crystallization exotherms during cooling quantified the enthalpy release.
papers.mechanism: Cooling rate critically affects the microstructure: slow cooling yields complex crystalline phases, whereas rapid quenching promotes amorphization. Phosphorus and high mixing entropy contribute to enhanced glass-forming ability, influencing the melting/freezing behavior.

papers.title: Microstructure and Thermal Analysis of Metastable Intermetallic Phases in High-Entropy Alloy CoCrFeMo0.85Ni.
papers.approach: Thermal analysis using both differential thermal analysis (DTA) and DSC combined with microstructural characterization (SEM, EDX) and CALPHAD-based phase diagram predictions.
papers.findings: Identified key temperatures for phase transitions including melting, solidus, and liquidus points. Some discrepancies were noted between CALPHAD predictions and DTA measurements for FCC phase formation, suggesting challenges in modeling complex phase equilibria.
papers.mechanism: The interplay between eutectic reactions and intermetallic phase formation in the multi-component system governs the observed thermal responses and the measured fusion enthalpies.

papers.title: In-Situ Imaging of Molten High-Entropy Alloys Using Cold Neutrons.
papers.system: CoCrCu-based high-entropy alloys with Ni additions (yielding equiatomic CoCrCuNi)
papers.approach: Real-time neutron imaging in a high-temperature furnace to capture a movie-like series of radiographs during melting, mixing, and solidification processes.
papers.findings: Direct in-situ visualization confirmed that when Ni is added, the previously immiscible CoCrCu system remixes into a single-phase liquid upon melting. The imaging captured the progression from phase-separated liquids to a homogeneous melt and the subsequent solidification process.
papers.mechanism: Ni acts as a solubility pathway to overcome liquid immiscibility by facilitating enhanced mixing and suppressing phase separation in the melt.

established: Accurate determination of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting is achievable via complementary experimental techniques (e.g., DSC, DTA, high-temperature XRD) and in-situ imaging methods.
Atomistic simulations (MD and hybrid MC/MD) can capture the microscopic mechanisms of melting, such as grain boundary pre-melting and collective atomic rearrangements.
CALPHAD modeling, despite some discrepancies, provides a robust framework for predicting phase equilibria and fusion properties in multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Neutron imaging enables real-time observation of melting and liquid-phase mixing in multi-principal element alloys.

approaches_tried.approach: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with specialized potentials (2NN MEAM)
approaches_tried.outcome: Successfully identified two-stage melting mechanisms and grain size effects on melting behavior.

approaches_tried.approach: Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) and Differential Thermal Analysis (DTA)
approaches_tried.outcome: Provided quantitative measurements of heat capacity, melting enthalpy, and transition temperatures; revealed thermal versus configurational entropy contributions.
Quantified free energy changes during annealing and revealed the significant role of configurational entropy in lowering Gibbs free energy.

approaches_tried.approach: CALPHAD modeling integrated with phase diagram prediction
approaches_tried.outcome: Enabled rapid assessment of phase stability in complex alloys, though some predictions deviate from experimental observations.
Offered decisive visual evidence of liquid-phase mixing and phase separation dynamics during melting.

mechanisms: Grain-boundary pre-melting followed by collective atomic rearrangements driving the complete melting process.
The interplay between vibrational (thermal) entropy and configurational (mixing) entropy that determines solid-solution stability and fusion behavior.
Local chemical ordering (short-range clustering) significantly influences the balance of enthalpy and entropy during annealing.
Nonideal mixing effects in the liquid state can raise the effective melting temperature through enhanced energetic stabilization.
disagreements: CALPHAD predictions sometimes disagree with experimental DTA/DSC measurements, particularly in determining the precise transition temperatures and phase boundaries (e.g., in CoCrFeMo0.85Ni).
Estimates of fusion enthalpies and the contributions of thermal vacancies in liquid-phase properties still exhibit uncertainties.
Differences exist in the inferred role of configurational vs. thermal entropy in stabilizing various phases across different high-entropy alloy systems.
open_questions: How to extend and optimize both experimental (e.g., DSC/DTA, neutron imaging) and computational methods to efficiently predict and validate fusion properties across the entire high-entropy alloy family.
The quantitative impact of liquid-phase nonidealities and local structural fluctuations on fusion enthalpy and entropy remains to be fully elucidated.

What are the optimal conditions (e.g., heating rates, sample preparation, simulation parameters) for achieving reliable, high-throughput determination of melting characteristics in multicomponent systems?
How can discrepancies between CALPHAD-based predictions and direct experimental measurements be minimized?
opportunities: Combine in-situ neutron imaging with DSC/DTA under controlled conditions to cross-validate melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies, and volume changes at melting.
Develop improved interatomic potentials and faster hybrid MC/MD methods to capture multi-scale melting phenomena more accurately.
Integrate high-throughput CALPHAD calculations with experimental datasets to refine theoretical models for fusion properties in newly designed HEAs.

Employ data-driven materials informatics to correlate computational free-energy profiles with experimental melting and liquid-phase properties, guiding the design of alloys with tailored fusion characteristics.

directions.direction: High-throughput experimental characterization using integrated DSC/DTA, in-situ synchrotron XRD, and high-temperature imaging to simultaneously measure heat flow, diffraction (phase changes), and volumetric changes during melting in HEAs.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets the measurement of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume change all in one integrated experiment. It leverages established techniques (DSC/DTA as shown in PMC7513177 and in-situ imaging as in PMC8320920) and minimizes ambiguities through simultaneous measurement. Its physics‐based rationale relies on the detection of latent heat (endothermic peaks) and corresponding structural transitions, yielding quantitative performance with expected accuracies (e.g., ±10 K for melting temperature, ±5 kJ/mol for latent heat) over a wide range of HEAs. The primary challenges are sample oxidation and instrumental calibration, which are manageable with inert atmospheres and proper protocols.

directions.direction: Atomistic modeling with molecular dynamics and hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations to compute melting behavior and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
directions.assessment: Atomistic simulations have been successfully used to examine melting mechanisms (e.g., PMC8956691). They provide microscopic insights into latent heat, pre-melting and atomic rearrangements. However, accuracy depends on the interatomic potentials and computational resources. Although they directly probe mechanisms, scaling to cover the entire HEA family could be challenging and may require extensive validation against experiments.

directions.direction: High-throughput CALPHAD modeling integrated with automated experimental calibration to predict and then refine fusion properties in multicomponent HEAs.
directions.assessment: CALPHAD methods are proven for assessing phase equilibria across many systems, as evidenced in several studies (e.g., PMC7412006). They offer rapid evaluation and prediction over wide composition spaces. That said, discrepancies exist between CALPHAD predictions and experimental DSC/DTA measurements in some systems, so calibration is essential. This strategy is efficient but may be limited by uncertainties in database extrapolations.

directions.direction: In-situ neutron imaging of molten HEAs to track the liquid-phase mixing and volume change concurrently with independent calorimetric analysis.
directions.assessment: Neutron imaging offers unique real-time insights into melting and phase segregation phenomena, as shown in PMC8320920. It can capture the dynamics of volume change and miscibility. However, due to its complexity and the requirement for specialized facilities, its throughput may be lower and its general applicability across all HEAs limited.

directions.direction: Data-driven materials informatics combining existing experimental and simulation datasets to build surrogate models for predicting melting temperatures, latent heats, and liquid-phase behaviors in HEAs.
directions.assessment: This strategy harnesses large-scale data to correlate fusion properties with alloy compositions and processing conditions. It is highly efficient and scalable across the vast HEA composition space, but it relies on the quality of the input data and may obscure underlying physical mechanisms. The approach is promising but requires rigorous validation.

choice.direction: High-throughput experimental characterization using integrated DSC/DTA, in-situ synchrotron XRD, and high-temperature imaging.
choice.why: This direction directly addresses the need to accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, as well as volume changes and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across the HEA family. By combining complementary measurement techniques into a single, integrated experimental framework, it leverages well-established physics (latent heat absorption, diffraction-based phase identification, and image-based volume tracking) and has demonstrated success in similar systems (supported by PMC7513177 and PMC8320920). The method ensures robustness and cross-validation, essential for spanning a broad range of HEA compositions while minimizing systematic errors.
